concept.body: Two centers, don't swap them. CIRCUMcenter: from PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS, equidistant from VERTICES, center of the circle AROUND (circumscribed). INcenter: from ANGLE BISECTORS, equidistant from SIDES, center of the circle INSIDE (inscribed). Circum→around→vertices; in→inside→sides.

explanationVariants: The incenter (angle bisectors) is equidistant from the SIDES.
In→inside→sides: the incenter's equal distances are to the three sides.

widget.prompt: The incenter is equidistant from the triangle's…

options.label: sides
options.feedback: Angle bisectors make the incenter equidistant from the three sides — center of the inscribed circle.

options.label: vertices
options.feedback: Equidistance from VERTICES is the CIRCUMcenter. The incenter is equidistant from SIDES.

options.label: medians
options.feedback: Medians relate to the centroid, and the incenter's equal distances are to SIDES, not medians.

options.label: altitudes
options.feedback: Altitudes make the orthocenter. The incenter is equidistant from the SIDES.

steps.body: Three lines of the same type in a triangle often meet at a single point — they're **concurrent**. The **circumcenter** is where the three **perpendicular bisectors** of the sides meet. Because every point on a side's perpendicular bisector is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, the meeting point is equidistant from all three vertices.

widget.prompt: The circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors' meeting point) is equidistant from which parts of the triangle?

options.label: the three vertices
options.feedback: Each perpendicular bisector keeps points equidistant from two vertices; their common point is equidistant from all three.

options.label: the three sides
options.feedback: Equidistance from SIDES is the incenter's property. Perpendicular bisectors give equidistance from VERTICES.

options.label: the three midpoints
options.feedback: The bisectors pass THROUGH the midpoints, but the circumcenter is equidistant from the VERTICES, not the midpoints.

options.label: the three angle bisectors
options.feedback: Angle bisectors define a different center (the incenter). The circumcenter comes from perpendicular bisectors.

explanationVariants: Equidistant from all three vertices, the circumcenter is the center of the circle PASSING THROUGH them — the circumscribed circle.
A circle centered at the circumcenter with radius to any vertex passes through all three — the circumcircle.

widget.prompt: Since the circumcenter is equidistant from all three vertices, it is the center of…

options.label: the circle passing through all three vertices (the circumscribed circle)
options.feedback: Equal distance to each vertex means one circle, centered there, hits all three — the circumcircle.

options.label: the circle touching all three sides
options.feedback: That inscribed circle is centered at the INCENTER. The circumcenter's circle passes through the VERTICES.

options.label: the largest circle that fits inside
options.feedback: The largest inscribed circle sits at the incenter. The circumcenter's circle goes AROUND, through the vertices.

options.label: no circle in particular
options.feedback: It's exactly the circumscribed circle's center — equidistance from the vertices defines it.

steps.body: The **incenter** is the other equidistance center: where the three **angle bisectors** meet. Every point on an angle's bisector is equidistant from the two SIDES forming that angle, so the common point is equidistant from all three sides — the center of the inscribed circle that just touches each side.

widget.prompt: The incenter (angle bisectors' meeting point) is equidistant from which parts?

options.label: the three sides
options.feedback: Each angle bisector keeps points equidistant from two sides; their meeting point is equidistant from all three.

options.label: the three vertices
options.feedback: Equidistance from VERTICES is the circumcenter. Angle bisectors give equidistance from SIDES.

options.label: only two sides
options.feedback: All THREE bisectors meet at the incenter, so it's equidistant from all three sides, not just two.

options.label: the midpoints of the sides
options.feedback: Midpoints relate to perpendicular bisectors. The incenter is equidistant from the SIDES themselves.

explanationVariants: Equidistant from all three sides, the incenter is the center of the circle that touches (is inscribed in) each side.
The inscribed circle sits at the incenter, its radius the common distance to the three sides.

widget.prompt: The incenter is the center of…

options.label: the inscribed circle, which touches all three sides
options.feedback: Equal distance to each side is the radius of the circle nestled inside, touching all three — the incircle.

options.label: the circle through the three vertices
options.feedback: That's the circumscribed circle at the CIRCUMCENTER. The incenter's circle touches the SIDES from inside.

options.label: a circle centered at a vertex
options.feedback: The incenter sits INSIDE the triangle, not at a vertex — it centers the inscribed circle.

options.label: no circle at all
options.feedback: It's precisely the inscribed circle's center — equidistance from the sides gives that circle's radius.

steps.body: A tale of two centers: **circumcenter** = perpendicular bisectors = equidistant from VERTICES = circle AROUND. **Incenter** = angle bisectors = equidistant from SIDES = circle INSIDE. The incenter always sits inside the triangle; the circumcenter can fall outside (for an obtuse triangle) since it only cares about vertex distances.

widget.prompt: Match each center to the lines that create it.

pairErrors.feedback: Angle bisectors make the INCENTER. The circumcenter comes from PERPENDICULAR BISECTORS.
Perpendicular bisectors make the CIRCUMCENTER. The incenter comes from ANGLE BISECTORS.

widget.missFeedback: Circumcenter ↔ perpendicular bisectors (vertices); incenter ↔ angle bisectors (sides).

hints: The town wants to be the same distance from three towers (points). Which center?
Equal distance from three POINTS (vertices) is the circumcenter's property.
Perpendicular bisectors give equidistance from vertices — the circumcenter.
explanationVariants: Equal distance from three fixed POINTS is exactly the circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors, equidistant from vertices).
Three points to be equidistant from → circumcenter, the circumscribed-circle center.

widget.prompt: You want a location equidistant from three towns (treat them as three points). Which triangle center solves this?

options.label: the circumcenter
options.feedback: Equidistant from three POINTS (vertices) is the circumcenter — the perpendicular-bisector meeting point.

options.label: the incenter
options.feedback: The incenter is equidistant from the SIDES, not from three points. For equal distance to points, use the circumcenter.

options.label: the centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the balance point, not an equal-distance point. Equidistance from vertices is the circumcenter.

options.label: the orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter (altitudes) has no equidistance property. Equal distance from three points is the circumcenter.

takeaways: Circumcenter: perpendicular bisectors meet; equidistant from vertices; center of circumscribed circle.
Incenter: angle bisectors meet; equidistant from sides; center of inscribed circle.
Incenter is always inside; circumcenter can fall outside an obtuse triangle.
steps.teaser: Next: the centroid and orthocenter — the balance point and the altitudes' meeting point.
